title: The Way We Were
bodyHtml:
Languages are constantly changing. For example, when you talk to your friends, you probably use some words that did not exist ten years ago. Even the basic grammar of a language can change.

Over time, these changes accumulate until new languages are born. In this way, the English that is spoken today—known as Present Day English—is descended from a language called Old English, which was spoken approximately a thousand years ago. Since that time, the language has transformed so much that, if you wanted to understand Old English, you would need to study it as a foreign language. This problem focuses on some of the differences between Old English and Present Day English.

Study the table below, which contains some sentences in Old English along with their translations in Present Day English. (The pronunciation of the letters is not important for this problem, but see the end of the problem for pronunciation notes.) Then answer the questions that follow.

Old EnglishPresent Day English
1.Æþelwine and Wulfstan gesawon þas menn. Hi hi gretton.Athelwine and Wulfstan saw these men. They greeted them.
2.Nereþ hit us?Does it save us?
3.Se cyning and se bisceop and ic gesawon þone arcebisceop. We hine gretton.The king and the bishop and I saw the archbishop. We greeted him.
4.Hwæt cweþe we?What do we say?
5.Seo lar eow nereþ.The teaching saves you.
6.We cumaþ.We come.
7.Ne hiere we þas wifmen.We do not hear these women.
8.þas weras hieraþ þas wifmen. Ne gesawon hi hi.These men hear these women. They did not see them.
9.þu hierdest þas menn.You heard these men.
10.þa hierde we þe.Then we heard you.
11.þu þe hierdest, and we us hierdon.You heard yourself, and we heard ourselves.
12.Alfred cyning and se bisceop ridon into þære byrig. þa gesawe we hi.King Alfred and the bishop rode into the town. Then we saw them.
13.Eadweard hine geseah. Gesawe ge us?Edward saw himself. Did you see us?
14.Hwæt fremest þu?What do you perform?
15.Fremede we hit?Did we perform it?

A1

Fill in the blank cells from the table below:

Old EnglishPresent Day English

A2

Fill in the blanks in these Old English sentences. A blank can be filled in with one word or a sequence of multiple words. For some blanks, there may be more than one solution; you should only give one.

Old EnglishPresent Day English
24.Ne grette ge _____(a)_____ .You did not greet them.
25.Seo lar hi _____(b)_____ .The teaching saves them.
26.Þu _____(c)_____ .You heard it.
27.Þa _____(d)_____ .Then they heard us.

Here are some more Old English sentences:

Old EnglishPresent Day English
28.Wit hieraþ þæt word and wit hit cweþaþ.We hear the word and we say it.
29.Se cyning and ic gesawon þas boceras, ac ne grette wit hi. þas boceras unc gretton.The king and I saw these scribes but we did not approach them. These scribes greeted us.
30.þonne cume wit to his rice.Then we come to his kingdom.
31.Æþelbald and ic eow gesawon, ac ne hierde wit eow. Wit eow gretton.Athelbald and I saw you, but we didn't hear you. We greeted you.
32.Edmund and Swiþun, ne hiere git þas wifmen, ac wit hi hieraþ. þas wifmen inc hieraþ.Edmund and Swithun, you do not hear these women, but we hear them. These women hear you.

A3

Below on the left are six Old English sentences which can all be translated into Present Day English by the single sentence We saw you. Match each Old English sentence with the context (on the right) in which it might have been said.

Old English
i.Wit eow gesawon.
ii.Wit inc gesawon.
iii.We eow gesawon.
iv.We inc gesawon.
v.We þe gesawon.
vi.Wit þe gesawon.
Context
A.I said “We saw you” to tell your people that my people and I had seen them.
B.Mother said “We saw you” to tell me that she and my father had seen me.
C.One bishop said “We saw you” to tell the archbishop that all the bishops had seen him.
D.I said “We saw you” to tell my sister and brother that my mother and I had seen them.
E.Athelbald said “We saw you” to tell Swithun and Edmund that he and his men had seen them.
F.The king said “We saw you” to tell the people that he and his queen had seen them all.

A4

Six distinct words are used to translate the Present Day English word you into Old English. For each of the following sentences, write the correct you word that is missing.

Old EnglishPresent Day English
33.Ne hierdest ___(a)___ hi.(Speaking to Paul) You didn't hear them.
34.Ne hierde ___(b)___ hi.(Speaking to Alfred & Edmund) You didn't hear them.
35.Æþelwine and Wulfstan, gesawon hi ___(c)___ ?Athelwine and Wulfstan, did they see you?
36.Hierde ___(d)___ hine?(Addressing the crowd) Did you hear him?
37.Paulus, gretton hi ___(e)___ ?Paul, did they greet you?
38.Gretton hi ___(f)___ ?(Speaking to Alfred, Athelwine, and Paul) Did they greet you?

Some more information about Old English

If someone referred to Old English, would you think of the language of Shakespeare, who was active at the end of the sixteenth century and the beginning of the seventeenth, or possibly of Geoffrey Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, written circa 1385? In the standard historical division of English, Shakespeare's language is actually Early Modern English, while Chaucer was writing late Middle English. English was brought to England from Germany and northern Denmark in the early fifth century, and before the conversion of the English to Christianity, was occasionally written in inscriptions using the Germanic runic alphabet. A small number of English writings in the Latin alphabet appear circa 700, but it is only in the ninth century that we find a substantial body of texts. The Old English (also known as Anglo-Saxon) period extended to circa 1100, when enough changes to the language had happened that it would be unintelligible to the people who brought the language to England. If Old English would have been incomprehensible to the speakers of the Middle English period, this is even more true for Present Day English speakers.

Additional notes

  • For the most part, Latin letters were used to represent similar sounds in Old English. The letter <æ> (which is capitalized as <Æ>) represented a vowel similar to that in Present Day English hat. The symbol <þ>, called thorn, comes from the runic alphabet and was used to represent sounds not found in Latin, the two sounds of <th> in Present Day English this and thigh.
  • Word order in Old English was flexible. In your answers for this problem, you should only use the word orders illustrated in the example sentences.

hints.text: Start by making a list of every Old English pronoun in the data and what it corresponds to in the translation. Pay attention to two things at once: who the pronoun refers to, and whether it is the doer of the action or the one the action is done to.

Old English pronouns distinguish three numbers, not two: exactly one person, exactly two people, and three or more. They also change shape depending on their job in the sentence (subject versus object). Separately, watch the word order: it is not always the same. Compare where the object sits when it is a full noun phrase (like "these men") with where it sits when it is a pronoun, and notice what happens when the sentence begins with ne ("not"), þa/þonne ("then") or a wh-word.

Work through sentence 32 as practice. Edmund and Swithun are two people, and the sentence begins with ne, so the order is ne + verb + subject + object: ne hiere git þas wifmen. The speaker and one companion are the "we" here, and that dual subject is wit. In the last clause the women are the subject and "you two" is the object, so the object form inc appears before the verb because it is a pronoun: þas wifmen inc hieraþ. That gives you both the subject form (git) and the object form (inc) of the two-person "you".

explanationHtml:
What is going on in this problem

Old English is the ancestor of the English we speak, but a thousand years of change have hidden two systems that were once obvious: a rich set of pronouns and a flexible but rule-governed word order. Almost every answer in this problem comes from those two systems.

Step 1: build the pronoun chart

Go through the data and write down each pronoun with its translation and its job in the sentence. "Subject" means the doer (the we in we saw); "object" means the one acted on (the us in they saw us).

From sentences 3, 6, 7, 11 and 12 you get ic = I, we = we (subject), us = us (object). From 9, 10, 11 you get þu = you (subject, one person) and þe = you (object, one person). Sentence 13, Gesawe ge us? "Did you see us?", gives ge as a subject "you", and sentence 5, Seo lar eow nereþ, gives eow as an object "you". So there are already two different "you" words for one person and two more for a group.

The extra sentences 28-32 add the surprise. In 29, "the king and I" are the subject and the sentence continues ne grette wit hi — wit means "we", but only when "we" is exactly two people. The matching object form appears in the same example: þas boceras unc gretton, "these scribes greeted us (two)". In 32, Edmund and Swithun are addressed as git when they are the subject and inc when they are the object.

This gives a three-way number system, called dual for the "exactly two" forms:

onetwo (dual)three or more
"I / we" subjecticwitwe
"me / us" object—uncus
"you" subjectþugitge
"you" objectþeinceow

Those six "you" forms are exactly what part A4 asks about. Third person is similar: hi is "they" and also "them", hine is "him", hit is "it".

Step 2: work out the word order

Compare these:

  • þas weras hieraþ þas wifmen — subject, verb, object. The object is a full noun phrase.
  • We hine gretton — subject, object, verb. The object is a pronoun, and it jumps in front of the verb.
  • Ne hiere we þas wifmen and þa hierde we þe — when the sentence starts with ne "not" or þa/þonne "then", the verb comes straight after it and the subject follows the verb.
  • Hwæt cweþe we? — wh-word, verb, subject.
  • Fremede we hit? — a yes/no question puts the verb first.

Step 3: apply it to A1

For (a), sentence 3 has þone arcebisceop "the archbishop", so the noun itself is arcebisceop. For (b), sentence 12 shows the pattern Alfred cyning = "King Alfred": the title goes after the name, so "King Edward" is Eadweard cyning. Both menn and weras translate as "men" (Old English had more than one word for it). Sentences 20-23 are then straight translations using the chart: Ne hierde ge hi has plural subject ge and object hi, and ne plus the past tense gives "did not", so it means "You did not hear them."

Step 4: A2, filling Old English blanks

Work backwards from the English. "The teaching saves them" has a pronoun object, so the order is subject-object-verb: Seo lar hi + the verb. Sentence 5 gives that verb as nereþ. "You heard it" likewise puts the pronoun object first: Þu hit hierdest, with the second-person singular past ending -est copied from sentence 9. "Then they heard us" starts with "then", so the verb comes next, then the subject, then the object: Þa hierdon hi us.

Step 5: A3, matching the contexts

Each sentence is "we saw you". You only need two questions: how many people are in the "we", and how many in the "you"? wit = we two, we = we three or more; þe = you one, inc = you two, eow = you three or more. Context B, "Mother said it to tell me that she and my father had seen me", is two speakers and one addressee, so it is Wit þe gesawon. Context C, one bishop speaking for all the bishops to a single archbishop, is many speakers and one addressee: We þe gesawon. Every context sorts out the same way.

Step 6: A4

Decide subject or object, then count. In 33 the blank is the subject and Paul is one person: þu. In 34 the subject is two people: git. In 35 the blank is the object (the addressees are Athelwine and Wulfstan, two people): inc. In 36 the crowd is the subject: ge. In 37 Paul is the object: þe. In 38 three addressees as object: eow.

One extra detail

You may have noticed gesawe we hi in 12 but gesawon elsewhere. When a first- or second-person plural pronoun follows the verb immediately, the verb ending shrinks to -e. That is why sentence 34 has hierde git rather than hierdon git. Present Day English kept only one "you" and lost the dual entirely — which is why the modern sentence "We saw you" is ambiguous in six different ways at once.
